description: Women's exclusion from formal politics in Athens and Rome, and the informal power they could still exercise.
content_html:
Excluded from the Assembly

In classical Athens, political decisions were made by the Ekklesia, the citizen assembly. Any adult male citizen could attend, speak, and vote. Women, slaves, and foreigners were entirely excluded. This was not an oversight: it was a deliberate feature of Athenian democratic ideology, which linked political participation to the qualities of a citizen warrior. Since women did not fight, they were not citizens in the full sense, and they had no voice in the governance of the city that their labour sustained. The philosopher Aristotle, writing in the late fourth century BC, argued that women were naturally suited to the domestic sphere and that their reason was less authoritative than men’s — a view that informed, and was reinforced by, their exclusion from political life.

Aristophanes and the Comic Inversion

The Athenian playwright Aristophanes wrote a comedy called the Assemblywomen (performed around 391 BC), in which a group of Athenian women, led by the resourceful Praxagora, disguise themselves as men, infiltrate the assembly, and pass a law giving women control of the city. The play is prescribed reading for this topic. In the opening section (lines 1–240), we see Praxagora rehearsing her fellow women in how to adopt male mannerisms and speak like citizens. The comedy works precisely because the premise is absurd to an Athenian audience: women running the city is funny because it inverts the natural order entirely. Yet the play is also a pointed satire on the failures of male-run democracy. Aristophanes is not seriously advocating for women’s equality; he is using the device of female rule to mock the incompetence of real Athenian politicians.

The literary source is valuable as evidence precisely for what it assumes: the audience’s automatic understanding that women in politics is ridiculous. That shared assumption tells us a great deal about Athenian cultural attitudes. It also raises questions for students of the ancient world: does the fact that a male author imagined women as capable leaders (however comically) suggest some underlying anxiety about gender and power?

Key Fact

Aristophanes’ Assemblywomen (c.391 BC) depicts women disguising themselves as men to take control of the Athenian assembly. The comedy is only funny if the audience finds women in politics inherently absurd — making it a key piece of evidence for Athenian attitudes towards female political participation.

The Trial of Agnodice

The story of Agnodice is told by the Roman author Hyginus (in his Fabulae) and serves as a significant prescriptive source for this topic. According to the story, Athenian women were suffering from lack of medical care because they were too embarrassed to be treated by male doctors. Agnodice disguised herself as a man, studied medicine, and began practising. When she was accused of seducing female patients, she revealed her sex in court. She was then prosecuted for practising medicine while female — because Athenian law apparently forbade women from doing so. Her female patients rallied to her defence, and the law was changed to allow women to practise medicine for women. The story is almost certainly a legend rather than a historical fact, but it is important evidence for ancient ideas about what women were and were not permitted to do professionally, and for the idea that male-authored narratives could occasionally present women as agents of change.

The seclusion of respectable Athenian women did not mean they had no influence at all. As household managers, wealthy women oversaw budgets, supervised slaves, and made practical decisions that kept the oikos (household economy) functioning. The best-known Athenian woman who challenged these boundaries is Aspasia, the companion of Pericles. Ancient authors — including the hostile comic poets and the philosopher Plato — credited Aspasia with influencing Pericles’ political speeches and even with teaching rhetoric. Because she was not an Athenian citizen (she was from Miletus), she was not subject to the same rules of seclusion, and she reportedly held intellectual conversations with prominent men. Plutarch’s Life of Pericles (chapter 24), a prescribed source, notes that she was prosecuted on charges of impiety and corrupting Athenian women — charges that suggest powerful men felt threatened by her influence.

Women and Roman Politics

The Roman Senate was, like the Athenian assembly, an exclusively male body. Roman women could not vote in the popular assemblies, stand for magistracies, or sit in the Senate. Yet Roman women — particularly those of the aristocracy — had more daily freedom of movement than their Athenian counterparts. They attended dinner parties alongside their husbands, visited temples and public spaces, and were visible in the life of the city in a way that respectable Athenian women were not.

The historian Livy records a remarkable episode: the repeal of the Oppian Law. In 195 BC, groups of Roman women gathered in public and approached male citizens to lobby for the repeal of this wartime sumptuary law. The conservative senator Cato the Elder argued fiercely against repeal, insisting that women needed to be controlled and that their public lobbying was an affront to male authority. He lost. The women’s campaign was successful. Livy presents the episode with some ambivalence — he clearly shares some of Cato’s discomfort about female public action — but the bare fact of the story is that Roman women engaged in collective political action and succeeded.

Key Fact

In 195 BC, Roman women publicly lobbied for the repeal of the Oppian Law, a sumptuary restriction imposed during wartime. Despite Cato the Elder’s fierce opposition, the law was repealed. This demonstrates that Roman women could exercise real collective influence in the political sphere, even though they held no formal political rights.

Sempronia and Political Conspiracy

The historian Sallust, in The Conspiracy of Catiline (chapters 24–25), paints a vivid portrait of Sempronia, an aristocratic woman of remarkable education and talent who was allegedly involved in Catiline’s conspiracy to overthrow the Roman Republic in 63 BC. Sallust describes her as literate in both Greek and Latin, skilled in music and dance, witty in conversation, and possessed of great personal charm. He also accuses her of shamelessness and recklessness, suggesting she craved excitement and excitement made her dangerous. Whether or not Sempronia was genuinely involved in the conspiracy is unclear, but Sallust’s account tells us much about Roman anxiety surrounding educated, independently minded women. Her intelligence and social access, the very qualities that made her admirable in a man, are presented as making her threatening in a woman.

Almost every literary source we have for women in the ancient world was written by men. This matters enormously. When Sallust describes Sempronia’s intelligence alongside her alleged immorality, he is not writing a neutral biography; he is constructing a type: the dangerously clever woman. When Aristophanes puts women in the assembly and makes them figures of comedy, he is not reporting facts but deploying cultural anxieties. Even the sympathetic sources, such as the Laudatio Turiae (a funeral inscription praising a Roman wife for her loyalty during the civil wars), are composed by husbands who celebrate what they valued in women — loyalty, chastity, self-sacrifice — rather than what women valued in themselves. Material sources such as the Parthenon Frieze or the Hegeso Stele can provide a counter-balance by showing women in their own spaces and roles, but they too were commissioned or carved by others. The honest approach is to acknowledge the bias and use it as evidence itself.
exam_tip_html: When a question asks you to ‘Explain’ or assess how far women had power, the key move is to distinguish between formal power (the right to vote, hold office, speak in the assembly — which women never had) and informal power (influence over a husband, collective lobbying, access to influential circles — which some women clearly exercised). Use the Oppian Law episode from Livy as evidence of collective action, Aspasia from Plutarch’s Pericles as individual influence, and Sempronia from Sallust as the portrait of a woman whose power was seen as dangerous precisely because it was real. In source-analysis questions on Aristophanes’ Assemblywomen, always comment on what the comedy’s premise assumes about the audience’s expectations — not just what it says literally.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Women in both Athens and Rome were formally excluded from political institutions — the Athenian Ekklesia and the Roman Senate — but the degree of social freedom differed: Roman aristocratic women had considerably more public visibility than Athenian women.
  • Informal power was real: the Oppian Law episode shows Roman women successfully lobbying in public; Aspasia shows individual influence through proximity to power; Sempronia shows that ancient authors found educated, politically connected women unsettling precisely because they were effective.
  • The sources themselves — Aristophanes’ comedy, Sallust’s hostile portrait of Sempronia, Plutarch’s biography of Pericles — are all male-authored and must be read critically. They reveal as much about cultural anxieties as about women’s actual lives.

practice_questions.text: Name the Athenian comic playwright who wrote the Assemblywomen.
Describe what the repeal of the Oppian Law in 195 BC tells us about the position of women in Rome.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any three of: the Oppian Law was a wartime restriction limiting women's ownership of gold and use of carriages; Roman women gathered publicly and lobbied male citizens for its repeal; Cato the Elder opposed repeal, arguing women needed to be controlled; the women succeeded despite male opposition; the episode shows Roman women were capable of collective political action even without formal rights.

practice_questions.text:
Read the following passage, which paraphrases part of Aristophanes' Assemblywomen (lines 1–240):

'Praxagora rehearses her friends in how to speak in the assembly. She tells them to speak boldly like men, to hold their staffs firmly and not fidget. One woman worries she has spent so much time at home weaving that she does not know how to make a proper speech. Praxagora reassures her: what they have practised among themselves will serve well enough for the assembly.'

What does this passage suggest about Athenian attitudes towards women and politics? Use specific details from the passage in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A perceptive analysis using several details from the passage (women must disguise themselves as men; Praxagora's coaching implies women lack natural political skills; the reference to weaving locates women's proper sphere in the home; the humour depends on the premise being absurd). Links the details to the broader insight that the passage reveals Athenian cultural assumptions about gender: women in politics is funny precisely because it is unthinkable. May note that the women's eventual success in the play could be read as an implicit comment on male political failure. Reaches a supported judgement.
Secure: Uses at least two specific details from the passage and explains what each reveals about Athenian attitudes. Makes a clear point about the comedy's premise as evidence of exclusionary ideology.
Developing: Identifies one or two details and makes a basic observation, but the analysis of what the passage reveals is limited or undeveloped.
Emerging: Paraphrases the passage or makes only a general observation without engaging with specific details.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the story of Agnodice is significant as evidence for the position of women in ancient Athens.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying what the story tells: a woman disguised herself as a man to practise medicine. 1 mark for explaining the significance: women were apparently forbidden from practising medicine, demonstrating legal restrictions on women's professional roles. 1 mark for contextualising the source: it is a legend told by the Roman author Hyginus, not a historical record. 1 mark for a further point: the detail that Athenian women preferred being treated by a female doctor suggests they were embarrassed by male treatment, implying strong norms around bodily modesty; or, the claim that the law was changed suggests ancient stories could present women as agents of change.

practice_questions.text: How far do the sources suggest that women in Athens and Rome were powerless? Use a range of named sources in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained argument that engages directly with the evidence for both formal exclusion and informal power. Formal exclusion: women excluded from the Ekklesia (Aristophanes' Assemblywomen shows this assumption clearly) and the Roman Senate (Livy's account of Cato defending male authority). Informal power: Oppian Law episode (Livy) showing collective female action; Aspasia's influence (Plutarch, Pericles 24); Sempronia's role (Sallust, Catiline 24–25). May also draw on material sources: the Hegeso Stele showing a wealthy woman managing servants and possessions; the Parthenon Frieze showing women in a civic procession. Critically evaluates the bias of male-authored sources. Reaches a nuanced, supported judgement: women were formally powerless but informally some women exercised real influence, and the very anxiety evident in male sources suggests that influence was felt.
Secure: Discusses formal exclusion and gives examples of informal power with named sources. Makes a clear argument and reaches a conclusion, even if the source analysis is less critical.
Developing: Covers some relevant material but the argument is uneven; sources may be listed rather than analysed.
Emerging: Makes general points without consistent use of named sources or with only one culture covered.

practice_questions.text: How does Sallust's portrayal of Sempronia reflect Roman attitudes towards women who wielded power? Use details from his description in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A nuanced analysis that identifies the ambivalence in Sallust's description: he admires Sempronia's education (literate in Greek and Latin, skilled in music and rhetoric) but immediately associates these qualities with moral danger and recklessness. Explains how this reflects Roman anxiety about women who stepped outside their domestic role, and connects it to the broader pattern in ancient sources of presenting powerful women as threatening. Uses specific details from Sallust's account (her intelligence, her alleged involvement in the conspiracy, the combination of praise and condemnation). May note that Sallust's account cannot be taken at face value because his purpose is to highlight Catiline's degeneracy.
Secure: Identifies key details from Sallust's description and explains what they reveal about Roman attitudes. Makes a clear point about the relationship between female intelligence and perceived danger. Supports with named evidence.
Developing: Describes Sallust's portrayal but the analysis of what it reveals is limited or asserted without full support.
Emerging: Paraphrases Sallust without analysing what his characterisation reveals about Roman attitudes.

knowledge_checks.q: Which Athenian playwright wrote the Assemblywomen, a comedy about women disguising themselves as men to take control of the assembly?
What does Livy's account of the repeal of the Oppian Law demonstrate about Roman women?
options: Roman women had the right to vote in the Senate
Roman women successfully lobbied in public and achieved a political outcome
Roman women were completely powerless in public life
The Oppian Law had always permitted women to own gold

knowledge_checks.q: Sallust's portrait of _____ in The Conspiracy of Catiline describes an aristocratic woman who was educated, charming, and allegedly involved in political conspiracy.
The Athenian _____ was the democratic assembly of adult male citizens where laws were debated and voted on — women were entirely excluded.
Match each source to the episode or figure it provides evidence for:
right: Women disguise themselves as men to take over the Athenian assembly
Roman women lobby for repeal of the Oppian Law
Aspasia's influence on Pericles and prosecution for impiety
Portrait of Sempronia as educated but morally dangerous

flashcard_questions.a: Sallust was a male author with a political purpose; his description reveals cultural anxieties as much as Sempronia's reality.

glossary_terms.definition: The democratic assembly of adult male citizens at Athens, where laws were debated and voted on, from which women were entirely excluded.
An Athenian comic playwright of the fifth and fourth centuries BC, known for satirical plays including the Assemblywomen.
A legendary Athenian woman who disguised herself as a man to practise medicine and was tried for practising medicine while female.
A foreign-born woman from Miletus who lived with the Athenian statesman Pericles and was credited in ancient sources with political and rhetorical influence.
A Roman sumptuary law of 215 BC restricting women's ownership of gold and use of carriages, repealed in 195 BC after public lobbying by women.
The senior advisory council of Rome, consisting of former magistrates; an exclusively male body from which women were excluded.
An aristocratic Roman woman of the late Republic whom Sallust portrays as educated and charming but morally dangerous in her alleged involvement in the Catilinarian Conspiracy.
A marble grave relief from Athens commemorating a wealthy woman named Hegeso, showing her seated and examining jewellery from a box held by a slave girl.
